the development of hyperglycemic diabetes is preceded by β‐cell dysfunction, that this dysfunction is the critical factor that leads to the development of hyperinsulinemia and central adiposity, and that these abnormalities in turn are important contributors to the development of the Metabolic Syndrome.

β‐cell function is impaired in the Metabolic syndrome, that the degree of this impairment is closely correlated with hyperglycemia, and that hyperinsulinemia is the result of a curvilinear response of the pancreas to insulin resistance.

the Metabolic Syndrome is characterized by an increased prevalence of impaired β‐cell dysfunction and insulin resistance, and that the development of hyperglycemic diabetes is preceded by impaired β‐cell insulin secretion and insulin resistance.

the mechanisms of β‐cell dysfunction in Type 2 diabetics, and the interaction of insulin sensitivity, insulin secretion and hyperglycemia in subjects with and without the Metabolic Syndrome.

the pathophysiological basis of the Metabolic Syndrome, the relationship between the metabolic abnormalities of the Metabolic syndrome and the development of Type 2 diabetes, and the mechanisms of β‐cell dysfunction and the development of central obesity.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
β‐cell function is the critical pathophysiologic abnormality in the development of Type 2 diabetes.
β‐cell function is the primary defect in the Metabolic syndrome.
β‐cell function is the primary determinant in the development of hyperglycemic disorders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the β‐cell dysfunction is the critical pathophysiologic abnormality in the development of the hyperglycemic state.
the β‐cell dysfunction is the key to understanding the pathogenesis of hyperglycemic states in the Metabolic syndrome and that it is a critical factor in the development of Type 2 diabetes.

the β‐cell dysfunction in the Metabolic syndrome is an important predictor for the development of Type 2 diabetes, and that hyperglycemia represents a compensatory mechanism to maintain normal glucose homeostasis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pathophysiology of hyperglycemic Type 2 diabetes begins with a β‐cell defect, and that the development of Type 2 diabetes can be predicted by impaired β‐cell compensation for insulin resistance.
hyperglycemia in diabetes and the Metabolic Syndrome is a compensatory mechanism to maintain glucose homeostasis and that the primary abnormality in this process is β‐cell dysfunction.
the Metabolic Syndrome and Type 2 diabetes have a common pathophysiology and that β‐cell failure is a key factor in the development of both disorders.
